hw-security-001.question: Which best describes the problems addressed by hardware security?
choices: Problems with PC casings breaking easily
Problems where, even with bug-free software, secrets leak or control is subverted through circuit properties or physical behavior
Problems with software license fees
hw-security-001.explanation: Even when software is written correctly, secrets can leak or defenses can fail through speculative execution and caches added for performance, power and timing that vary with processing, malfunctions under abnormal voltage or temperature, or circuitry inserted during manufacturing. Hardware security deals with understanding the principles of these threats and countering them in circuit and system design.
choiceNotes: It is not about casing strength.
Correct. It deals with threats rooted in circuits and physics.
It is not about fees.

hw-security-002.question: Which describes a side-channel attack?
choices: An attack trying passwords head-on by brute force
An attack flooding a network to stop a service
An attack inferring secrets from physical information other than the intended output, such as processing time, power consumption or emitted electromagnetic waves
hw-security-002.explanation: Even if a cryptographic algorithm is mathematically secure, the circuit running it varies slightly in timing and power depending on the values it handles. A side-channel attack measures information leaking through these side paths and analyzes it statistically to infer secrets such as keys. Countermeasures make timing and power independent of secret values or hide the leakage with noise and randomness.
choiceNotes: That is a brute-force attack.
That is a denial-of-service attack.
Correct. It extracts information without breaking the cryptographic math itself.

hw-security-003.question: Which correctly pairs the principle behind timing attacks with a typical countermeasure?
choices: It exploits processing that is too fast; deliberately slow it down
It exploits an inaccurate clock time; synchronize the clock
It exploits processing time varying with secret values; implement code that takes the same time regardless of secrets (constant-time)
hw-security-003.explanation: In an implementation that does extra work only when a key bit is 1, for example, repeated timing measurements reveal the key bits. The countermeasure is constant-time code, where branches, loop counts and memory access locations do not depend on secrets. Merely slowing everything down or adding random delays is not enough, because attackers can average away the noise with more measurements.
choiceNotes: Uniformly slowing down still leaks if time differences remain.
It is not about clock time-of-day.
Correct. Branches and memory accesses must not depend on secrets.

hw-security-004.question: What weakness lurks in the password comparison function above, and what is the fix?
choices: Large n makes the result wrong; shrink n before comparing
It stops at the first mismatch, so processing time reveals how many leading characters match; compare to the end and return the combined result
There is no problem; it is safe as is
hw-security-004.explanation: The function returns immediately if the first character differs and only after checking the second if the first matches, so time grows with the number of matching characters. An attacker trying candidates one character at a time and keeping the slower ones can guess the password without trying every combination. Accumulating the differences of all characters, for example with XOR, and deciding at the end makes the time independent of how many characters match.
choiceNotes: The result is correct, but time leaks information.
Correct. The key is not to create timing differences.
It is vulnerable to timing attacks.

hw-security-005.question: What is the main reason cache-based side-channel attacks work?
choices: Caches can be shared between processes, so which data another process used can be observed as differences in one's own access speed (hit or miss)
Anyone can directly read the contents of a cache
Caches save data to disk unencrypted
hw-security-005.explanation: Cached data is read fast and uncached data slowly. If an attacker fills part of a shared cache with its own data and later times reads of it, it can tell whether another process used those locations and evicted its data. If cryptographic code reads different table locations depending on the key, key information leaks this way.
choiceNotes: Correct. Access time becomes a trace.
The contents are not read directly; they are inferred from timing.
Caches do not save to disk.

hw-security-006.question: What is the principle behind the speculative execution vulnerability known as Spectre?
choices: A CPU arithmetic error changes the results of additions
Instructions executed speculatively along a predicted branch are rolled back, but their traces in the cache remain and can be read by timing measurements
Speculative execution overheats the CPU
hw-security-006.explanation: CPUs execute instructions on the predicted side of a branch before its outcome is known and discard the results if the prediction was wrong. In Spectre, an attacker trains the predictor to mispredict, so a path that should never execute reads secret data and loads a cache location that depends on its value. The results are discarded but the cache state is not restored, so the value can be inferred through a cache side channel.
choiceNotes: Computational results are correctly rolled back.
Correct. A performance feature leaves traces.
It is not a temperature problem.

hw-security-007.question: Why does information still leak in attacks like Spectre even though speculatively executed instructions are rolled back?
choices: The rollback fails and secret values remain in registers
Speculative results are saved to disk
Only architectural state such as registers is rolled back; microarchitectural state such as caches is not restored
hw-security-007.explanation: CPUs are designed to fully restore program-visible state (registers and memory contents) on a misprediction. But microarchitectural state, such as cache contents and branch predictor state, is internal performance state and is not restored. The ISA contract is honored, yet internal state becomes visible from outside as timing differences; that is the essence of this class of vulnerability.
choiceNotes: Registers are correctly restored.
Nothing is saved to disk.
Correct. Only state visible through the ISA is restored.

hw-security-008.question: What is the principle of the vulnerability called Meltdown, which affected some CPUs?
choices: The CPU melts from heat and data leaks out
Even an instruction reading kernel memory without permission speculatively reads the value before the permission exception takes effect, leaving value-dependent traces in the cache
A misconfiguration exposing kernel memory to all processes
hw-security-008.explanation: When a user program tries to read kernel memory, it should take a permission exception and get no value. On affected CPUs, however, in the brief window before the exception took effect, later instructions using the loaded value ran speculatively and brought a value-dependent location into the cache. The results were discarded by the exception, but kernel data could be inferred through a cache side channel.
choiceNotes: Nothing physically melts.
Correct. The problem was the ordering of permission checks and speculative reads.
It was a CPU implementation issue, not a misconfiguration.

hw-security-009.question: What is the idea behind KPTI (kernel page-table isolation), introduced as a software countermeasure to Meltdown?
choices: While user programs run, most kernel memory is removed from the page tables so it cannot be read even speculatively
Encrypt the entire kernel and store it on disk
Forbid user programs from running
hw-security-009.explanation: For fast switching, traditional OSes mapped kernel memory into each user process's page tables, marked as inaccessible. Meltdown read it speculatively before that mark was checked, so KPTI removes kernel pages from the mapping altogether while user code runs. Without an address translation, the data cannot be read even speculatively. Switching page tables on every system call, however, costs performance.
choiceNotes: Correct. In exchange, switches such as system calls become heavier.
The kernel is not moved to disk.
Programs run normally.

hw-security-010.question: Which is NOT used as a countermeasure to speculative-execution vulnerabilities such as Spectre?
choices: Inserting barrier instructions that stop speculation after dangerous branches
Raising the CPU clock frequency
Masking array indices into range so out-of-bounds data cannot be read speculatively
hw-security-010.explanation: Countermeasures to Spectre include inserting instructions that halt speculation after conditional branches (such as x86 lfence), masking indices so out-of-range data cannot be read, coding patterns that prevent abuse of indirect branch prediction (such as retpoline) and CPU microcode updates that control predictors. Disabling all speculation would cripple performance, so these measures are usually applied only at dangerous locations.
choiceNotes: This is a real countermeasure.
Correct. Frequency is unrelated to speculation.
This is a real countermeasure.

hw-security-011.question: Which statement about countermeasures to speculative-execution vulnerabilities is generally correct?
choices: Countermeasures have no effect on performance at all
The more speculation and cache sharing are restricted, the safer it gets, but performance drops, so the choice balances security and performance
Removing speculation makes CPUs faster
hw-security-011.explanation: Speculative execution, branch prediction and shared caches underpin modern CPU performance. Restricting them reduces leakage but costs performance. So OS, compiler and CPU designers choose how far to go based on the information at stake and the severity of the threat. Newer CPUs increasingly build in countermeasures with little performance impact.
choiceNotes: Some workloads slow noticeably.
Correct. The very features that boost performance are the cause.
Speculation exists to raise performance.

hw-security-012.question: Among power analysis attacks on chips performing cryptography, what characterizes differential power analysis (DPA)?
choices: It collects many power traces and processes them statistically to extract small key-dependent differences invisible in a single trace
A single power trace viewed by eye reveals the whole key
It cuts the chip's power to extract the key
hw-security-012.explanation: CMOS circuits consume power when signals switch, so power varies slightly with the data processed. Simple power analysis reads the flow of processing from the shape of a single trace, whereas DPA collects traces from thousands of cryptographic operations and correlates them with intermediate values predicted for each key guess to find the right key. Its hallmark is extracting small differences buried in noise through statistics.
choiceNotes: Correct. Statistics bring small differences out of the noise.
That would be simple power analysis (SPA) in the ideal case.
Without power, nothing is processed.

hw-security-013.question: What is the idea behind masking, a countermeasure against power analysis?
choices: Covering the chip surface with tape to hide it
Intermediate values are combined with a fresh random number each time to hide them, breaking the link between power consumption and secret values
Using the same cryptographic key in every device
hw-security-013.explanation: Power analysis exploits correlations between intermediate values and power consumption. With masking, an intermediate value x is never handled directly but represented combined with a freshly generated random m (for example x XOR m), and the correct result is recovered at the end. The values the circuit actually handles change randomly each time, obscuring the correlation between power and secrets. Good randomness and circuit designs that never expose unmasked values are essential.
choiceNotes: It is not physical covering.
Correct. Even with the same key, different values are processed each time.
A shared key puts every device at risk if one is analyzed.

hw-security-014.question: What characterizes electromagnetic side-channel analysis?
choices: A small probe near the chip measures electromagnetic emissions from circuits and can sometimes capture location-specific detail
It can never be measured from any distance with any equipment
Electromagnetic emissions have no relation to secret information
hw-security-014.explanation: Switching currents inside a circuit create electromagnetic fields around it. Bringing a small coil probe close to the chip surface can measure current changes in specific parts, such as a cryptographic block, in more detail than whole-chip power. Countermeasures, as with power analysis, include masking and circuits that smooth power variation, plus shielding with metal layers.
choiceNotes: Correct. It can yield more localized information than power measurement.
Measurements from a distance have also been studied under some conditions.
Changing currents create emissions that carry information.

hw-security-015.question: Which describes a fault injection attack?
choices: An attack that briefly disturbs supply voltage or clock or shines a laser to make a chip malfunction, skipping authentication or inferring keys
The task of counting bugs in a program
A test finding chips broken by manufacturing defects
hw-security-015.explanation: Chips are designed to work correctly within specified voltage and clock ranges. A fault injection attack deliberately induces malfunctions by briefly dropping the supply voltage, inserting a short glitch into the clock, or applying a laser or electromagnetic pulse. It is known that this can skip a comparison instruction to bypass signature verification, or reveal keys by comparing faulty and correct cryptographic outputs.
choiceNotes: Correct. It deliberately induces malfunctions.
It is not bug counting.
Its purpose differs from manufacturing tests.

hw-security-016.question: Which is NOT a countermeasure against fault injection attacks?
choices: Placing sensors that detect voltage or clock anomalies and stopping when they trigger
Performing important checks only once to speed up processing
Computing critical results twice or verifying them inversely, withholding output on mismatch
hw-security-016.explanation: Fault injection tries to defeat protection with a single induced error, so a check performed only once becomes the weak point. Countermeasures include sensors for voltage, clock and light, redundancy that repeats critical computations or comparisons and cross-checks the results, and responses such as erasing keys when a fault is detected. Software also double-checks critical branches and uses success and failure codes that differ in many bits.
choiceNotes: This is an effective countermeasure.
Correct. A single check can be skipped by a single glitch.
This is an effective countermeasure.

hw-security-017.question: Which is a countermeasure against DRAM Rowhammer?
choices: Halving DRAM capacity
Refreshing rows adjacent to frequently activated rows early (such as TRR), or increasing the refresh rate
Stopping the CPU clock
hw-security-017.explanation: Rowhammer is the phenomenon in which activating a row many times in a short period causes electrical interference that drains charge from cells in neighboring rows, flipping bits. It could let unprivileged programs alter other processes' or kernel data. Countermeasures combine mechanisms that additionally refresh neighbors of heavily activated rows, higher refresh rates and ECC to detect and correct flips.
choiceNotes: Reducing capacity is not a countermeasure.
Correct. Cells are rewritten before their charge leaks away.
Stopping the clock halts operation.

hw-security-018.question: Which correctly pairs why cold boot attacks work with a typical countermeasure?
choices: DRAM erases instantly at power-off; keep the power on
Heating DRAM makes contents easier to read; add cooling
DRAM contents persist for seconds to minutes after power-off, longer when cooled; encrypt memory contents
hw-security-018.explanation: DRAM cell charge does not disappear immediately when refresh stops; contents largely persist for seconds to minutes, and longer at low temperature. Removing the memory from a just-powered-off PC and reading it elsewhere can reveal secrets such as disk encryption keys. Countermeasures include hardware memory encryption, erasing keys at shutdown and keeping keys only inside the CPU.
choiceNotes: The charge does not vanish instantly.
Cooling makes contents persist longer.
Correct. Encrypted contents are useless if read.

hw-security-019.question: Which describes secure boot?
choices: A mechanism to boot a PC quickly
At each boot stage, the digital signature of the next software is verified, and only authentic software is started
A mechanism that erases the disk at every boot
hw-security-019.explanation: In secure boot, immutable ROM code verifies the first bootloader's signature, that bootloader verifies the next stage or the OS kernel, and so on, forming a chain of trust. If any stage's signature fails, boot stops, so malware that rewrites the bootloader or OS boot code cannot run. It is widely used in smartphones, PCs and embedded devices.
choiceNotes: It is not for speed.
Correct. It prevents tampered software from starting.
It does not erase the disk.

hw-security-020.question: What is the most suitable thing placed inside the chip as the root of trust for secure boot?
choices: Immutable ROM boot code and the public key (or its hash) used to verify signatures
Boot code in flash memory that anyone can rewrite
The latest OS downloaded from the internet
hw-security-020.explanation: The chain of trust assumes the component performing the first check is correct. So the root of trust is boot code in mask ROM, written at manufacture and unchangeable afterward, together with the public key used to verify signatures (often stored as a hash in eFuses to save space). If this could be rewritten, every later check would be meaningless.
choiceNotes: Correct. The starting point must be unchangeable.
If the root can be rewritten, every check can be faked.
The root resides in an unchanging part of the chip.

hw-security-021.question: What is the advantage of using public-key cryptography to verify software signatures in secure boot?
choices: Devices need only the public key for verification, while the signing private key stays securely with the vendor, so analyzing a device does not enable forged signatures
Public-key cryptography is always faster than symmetric cryptography
The public key must be kept secret
hw-security-021.explanation: With symmetric verification, the verification key can also create signatures, so extracting it from one device could enable fake software for every device. With public-key cryptography, devices hold only a public key usable for verification, and the signing private key stays inside the vendor's secure facility. Knowing the public key does not allow forging signatures.
choiceNotes: Correct. There is no private key on the device to extract.
Public-key cryptography is generally slower.
The public key may be known without harm.

hw-security-022.question: In devices with secure boot, why is an anti-rollback mechanism needed?
choices: New software versions have no signature
Older versions take longer to boot
Older vulnerable software versions also carry valid signatures, so reverting to them enables attacks
hw-security-022.explanation: The vendor has signed older releases legitimately too, so signature checks alone would still boot an old version reinstalled after a vulnerability was found. Software therefore carries a version number, and the chip records in write-once storage such as eFuses a minimum version below which it refuses to boot. Advancing this number with each update prevents rollback to old versions.
choiceNotes: New versions are signed too.
It is not about speed.
Correct. Version numbers kept in unchangeable storage are compared.

hw-security-023.question: What is the main role of a TPM (Trusted Platform Module) installed in PCs and similar?
choices: A dedicated circuit to speed up display
A component managing CPU cooling
Securely generating and storing keys, recording measurements of booted software and attesting to that state, among other security functions
hw-security-023.explanation: A TPM is a tamper-resistant security chip (or a function built into the CPU) that generates and stores keys, performs cryptographic operations, generates random numbers and records hashes of booted software. For example, releasing the disk encryption key only when the boot state is correct makes data hard to read even if the disk is removed or boot software is altered.
choiceNotes: It is not a display circuit.
It is not a cooling component.
Correct. It also protects keys such as disk encryption keys.

hw-security-024.question: What is the difference between secure boot and measured boot?
choices: They are the same thing under different names
Secure boot stops incorrect software from starting; measured boot records hashes of booted software in a TPM or similar so the state can be checked later
Measured boot merely measures how long booting takes
hw-security-024.explanation: In measured boot, each stage hashes the next piece of software and records it cumulatively in TPM registers (PCRs). A PCR can only be updated by combining its previous value with a new hash, so records cannot be forged. Boot itself is not stopped, but the recorded values let one later confirm which software started, or prove it to a remote server.
choiceNotes: They differ in stopping versus recording.
Correct. They are often used together.
It measures software contents, not time.

hw-security-025.question: Which describes remote attestation?
choices: A remote person viewing and operating the device's screen
Reporting the device's location to a server via GPS
A device presents the state of its running software, signed with a key inside its chip, to a remote server, which then judges whether it can be trusted
hw-security-025.explanation: In remote attestation, a device signs software measurements recorded in its TPM or TEE with a key that cannot be extracted from the chip and sends them to a server. The server checks the signature and measurements and grants secret data or services only to devices running approved software. It is used when entrusting confidential computation to the cloud or vetting devices joining corporate networks.
choiceNotes: It is different from remote control.
It is not location reporting.
Correct. It uses records such as those from measured boot.

hw-security-026.question: Which describes a TEE (trusted execution environment)?
choices: A hardware-protected execution environment isolated even from the normal OS, used for critical work such as key handling and authentication
An environment for speeding up internet traffic
A text editor for writing programs
hw-security-026.explanation: A normal OS is large and complex, so eliminating vulnerabilities completely is difficult. A TEE uses hardware mechanisms to create a small execution environment separated from the normal OS, where especially sensitive tasks run, such as fingerprint matching, payment processing and handling DRM keys. The goal is that even if the normal OS is compromised, the TEE's memory and keys remain out of reach. Arm TrustZone is a representative example.
choiceNotes: Correct. It protects its secrets even if the OS is compromised.
It is unrelated to network speed.
It is not an editor.

hw-security-027.question: What is the basic mechanism of Arm TrustZone?
choices: All secure processing runs on a separate PC
Normal-world programs can freely read secure-world memory
The CPU has secure-world and normal-world states, and bus signals distinguish which world each memory or peripheral access comes from, enforcing restrictions
hw-security-027.explanation: In TrustZone, a CPU core switches between secure and normal states, and every access carries a bus signal indicating which state issued it. Logic on the memory and peripheral side checks this signal and rejects normal-world accesses to regions assigned to the secure world. It creates a secure area within a single SoC without an extra chip, so it is widely used in smartphones and similar devices.
choiceNotes: The separation is within the same chip.
The normal world is prevented from reading it.
Correct. The same CPU is shared between two worlds.

hw-security-028.question: What characterizes enclave-style TEEs such as Intel SGX?
choices: The entire OS kernel runs from an external hard disk
Part of an application runs in a region whose memory the CPU encrypts and protects, so even the OS and hypervisor cannot read it
Anyone can freely modify data inside the enclave
hw-security-028.explanation: In an enclave, only the part of an application handling secrets runs in a special memory region, which the CPU encrypts before it reaches main memory (some implementations also detect tampering). Neither the OS, the hypervisor nor an attacker physically reading memory can see its contents. Only the CPU and that code need be trusted. Vulnerabilities to side-channel attacks have also been reported, so careful use is needed.
choiceNotes: It does not run from an external disk.
Correct. The trusted base shrinks to the CPU and part of the app.
Data inside is protected.

hw-security-029.question: In confidential computing on the cloud, what is the purpose of CPU features that encrypt virtual machine memory (such as AMD SEV or Intel TDX)?
choices: To always double virtual machine speed
To increase virtual machine memory capacity
To keep data inside a virtual machine unreadable even by the cloud provider's hypervisor and administrators
hw-security-029.explanation: Normally a virtual machine's memory can be freely read and written by the hypervisor running it, so users must trust the cloud provider. With memory encryption, per-VM keys are managed only inside the CPU, and memory contents stay encrypted outside it, hiding them from the hypervisor and from attackers reading memory directly. It is used together with remote attestation.
choiceNotes: Encryption may slow things slightly.
Capacity does not increase.
Correct. The aim is to avoid having to trust the infrastructure.

hw-security-030.question: Which describes a PUF (physically unclonable function)?
choices: A mechanism that uses per-chip manufacturing variation to produce values unique to each chip and hard to clone
A mechanism writing the same value into every chip
A product number printed on the chip surface
hw-security-030.explanation: Even chips of the same design differ slightly in transistor threshold voltages and wire delays due to manufacturing variation. A PUF reads out these differences to produce a value unique to each chip. Not even the manufacturer can control the variation, so producing a chip with the same value is very difficult. PUFs are used for device authentication and as a source for generating keys.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is like a fingerprint for the chip.
Values must differ from chip to chip.
A printed number is easy to copy.

hw-security-031.question: What is the advantage of using a PUF for key storage?
choices: Users can freely choose the key value
The key always remains in memory at power-off
The key need not be written in non-volatile memory and is regenerated only when used, so it is hard to extract even if the chip is analyzed
hw-security-031.explanation: Keys written in flash or eFuses are targets for attacks that open the chip and read storage directly. With a PUF, the key is regenerated from the chip's physical properties each time it is used and is stored nowhere while power is off. For some PUF types, physically tampering with the chip to read the PUF also alters the very variation it depends on, making extraction even harder.
choiceNotes: The value is set by variation and cannot be chosen.
Not storing it is precisely the advantage.
Correct. With power off, the key is stored nowhere.

hw-security-032.question: What property does an SRAM PUF exploit?
choices: Right after power-on, each SRAM cell tends to settle to 0 or 1 depending on transistor variation
SRAM retains data permanently with power off
Every SRAM cell always becomes 0 at power-on
hw-security-032.explanation: An SRAM cell is a pair of cross-coupled inverters, and which way it falls right after power-on is decided by slight strength differences between the transistors of the two inverters. So the pattern of initial values across cells is unique to each chip and reappears almost identically at every power-on. The advantage is that it uses SRAM most chips already have, with no special circuitry.
choiceNotes: Correct. The pattern of initial values is the chip's fingerprint.
SRAM is volatile.
If all were 0, there would be no fingerprint.

hw-security-033.question: Why is error correction (such as helper data) combined with PUFs when deriving keys?
choices: Some PUF output bits can change between readings due to temperature, voltage and noise, while the key must be exactly the same every time
Every PUF output bit inverts on each reading
Error correction automatically doubles the key length
hw-security-033.explanation: PUF values are set by manufacturing variation, but cells whose two options differ only slightly may read differently depending on temperature, voltage and noise. A cryptographic key is useless if even one bit differs, so at enrollment auxiliary information called helper data is created, and at each readout an error-correcting code fixes the fluctuating bits before the key is derived. Helper data is constructed so that it does not reveal the key itself.
choiceNotes: Correct. Small fluctuations are corrected before deriving the key.
Most bits stay the same each time.
It is not for lengthening the key.

hw-security-034.question: Which describes a true random number generator (TRNG) built into a chip?
choices: A program producing a random sequence from a seed with a fixed formula
A circuit generating random numbers from unpredictable physical phenomena such as thermal noise or oscillator jitter
A circuit using the clock time directly as a random number
hw-security-034.explanation: A pseudo-random sequence can be regenerated if its seed is known, so guessing the seed means guessing the keys. A TRNG generates bits from unpredictable physical phenomena such as resistor thermal noise or ring-oscillator period jitter. In practice, TRNG output often seeds a cryptographic pseudo-random generator, combining speed with unpredictability.
choiceNotes: That is a pseudo-random number generator.
Correct. It serves as the source for generating cryptographic keys.
Time is predictable and unsuitable as randomness.

hw-security-035.question: What can happen if poor-quality, predictable random numbers are used to generate cryptographic keys?
choices: Encryption becomes faster
Ciphertexts become twice as long
Even with a strong algorithm, the key can be guessed and the encryption broken
hw-security-035.explanation: Cryptographic security relies on attackers not knowing the key. If the random numbers used to make keys are biased, or not enough unpredictability has accumulated right after power-on, the space of possible keys shrinks and brute force can find them. Real cases have been reported in which flawed randomness left many devices with similar keys. Random number generation is one of the most fundamental building blocks of security.
choiceNotes: It has nothing to do with speed.
It has nothing to do with length.
Correct. Key unpredictability is the foundation of security.

hw-security-036.question: Which describes a hardware Trojan?
choices: Malicious circuitry inserted during design or manufacturing to leak information or disable operation
A dedicated circuit that removes software viruses
A clock circuit wired in a tree shape
hw-security-036.explanation: Modern chips are often designed by combining IP from many companies and manufactured in another company's fab, involving many organizations and people. Along the way, malicious circuitry could be added that, for example, leaks a key under some condition or stops operating at a set date. This is called a hardware Trojan. It cannot be removed by software updates after manufacturing, so countermeasures are needed across the entire design and manufacturing flow.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a malicious function hidden in the circuit.
It is not an antivirus circuit.
It is unrelated to clock trees.

hw-security-037.question: What is the main reason hardware Trojans are hard to find with ordinary testing?
choices: Hardware Trojans are attached outside the chip
Hardware Trojans destroy the test equipment
They are built to activate only under extremely rare inputs or conditions (triggers) and otherwise behave like normal circuits
hw-security-037.explanation: Manufacturing tests check that the designed functions work correctly. A hardware Trojan is built to activate only under conditions tests almost never produce, such as a particular 32-bit input value or a counter reaching billions, so it normally appears healthy. It may also need only a tiny number of transistors compared with billions in the whole chip, making visual detection difficult too.
choiceNotes: They hide among the circuits inside the chip.
They do not destroy equipment.
Correct. They trigger on conditions tests never produce.

hw-security-038.question: Which is NOT a countermeasure against hardware Trojans?
choices: Deleting the Trojan circuitry with a software update after shipping
Obtaining design data and IP only from trusted sources and strictly controlling changes
Comparing characteristics such as power and delay against known-good chips
hw-security-038.explanation: A hardware Trojan is built into the circuitry, so it cannot be removed after shipping. Countermeasures combine choosing trusted design tools, IP and foundries, logging and verifying changes to design data, deprocessing sample chips to compare with the design, comparing power and delay against known-good chips, and manufacturing critical portions in separate fabs.
choiceNotes: Correct. Circuits cannot be deleted by software.
This is an effective countermeasure.
This is an effective countermeasure.

hw-security-039.question: What is the danger of counterfeit chips (such as remarked parts) in the semiconductor supply chain?
choices: Used, defective or lower-grade chips relabeled as something else enter the supply, causing equipment failures, safety problems or malicious circuitry
Counterfeit chips are always higher-performing than genuine ones
Counterfeit chips turn genuine automatically if bought from a proper dealer
hw-security-039.explanation: Counterfeits include used parts pulled from scrapped equipment, sanded and remarked to look new, lower-grade parts (for example in temperature range) marked as higher grades, and entirely different chips. They may work at first but fail early or malfunction in harsh conditions, which is especially dangerous in aviation, automotive and medical uses. Prevention includes buying from authorized distributors, incoming inspection and chip authentication mechanisms.
choiceNotes: Correct. Buying through authorized channels is the basic countermeasure.
They are almost always inferior in performance or reliability.
They never turn genuine.

hw-security-040.question: Why are debug ports such as JTAG disabled or placed behind authentication in shipped products?
choices: Debug ports drain the battery by increasing power
Debug ports break automatically after shipping
Debug ports allow reading and writing memory and registers and halting programs, so left open they let firmware and keys be stolen or altered
hw-security-040.explanation: Debug ports such as JTAG and SWD are powerful tools for freely inspecting a chip during development. Left active in a product, an attacker can connect equipment to the board's pins and read out firmware, bypass secure boot or extract keys. Countermeasures include disabling them with eFuses at shipping or enabling them only after cryptographic authentication.
choiceNotes: Power is not the main reason.
They do not break automatically.
Correct. What helps development also helps attackers.

hw-security-041.question: Which describes the tamper resistance required of security chips such as smart cards?
choices: The property of not breaking when wet
The property of protecting internal secrets by making physical attacks such as opening the chip or probing difficult, and erasing keys when tampering is detected
The property of running fast at high temperature
hw-security-041.explanation: Tamper resistance is the ability to withstand attempts to extract secrets by deprocessing the chip or probing internal wiring. Countermeasures combine detecting cuts in a metal mesh (shield) covering the surface, detecting abnormal light, temperature or voltage, encrypting or scrambling internal buses and layout, and erasing keys when an anomaly is detected. Evaluation also covers resistance to side-channel and fault injection attacks.
choiceNotes: It is not waterproofing.
Correct. It is resistance against physical attack.
It is not about speed.

hw-security-042.question: Which method is commonly used to store keys written into a chip?
choices: One-time-programmable eFuses or OTP memory, or storing them encrypted in non-volatile memory
Printing the key value on the chip surface
Placing the key value as is in memory anyone can read externally
hw-security-042.explanation: An eFuse is one-time-programmable storage written bit by bit by blowing a thin wire with a large current. Per-device keys and settings are written after manufacturing, sometimes made unreadable by software so that only the cryptographic engine can use them. Another approach stores keys in flash encrypted with a key derived from a PUF. In every approach, restricting read paths is essential.
choiceNotes: Correct. Read restrictions and combination with PUFs are also used.
Anyone looking would see it.
The key would be stolen immediately.

hw-security-043.question: Besides speed, what advantage comes from giving CPUs dedicated AES instructions (such as AES-NI)?
choices: AES keys automatically become longer
It eliminates the table lookups used by software implementations, preventing cache-timing leaks caused by key-dependent memory accesses
Anyone can read AES ciphertext without the key
hw-security-043.explanation: Fast software AES often used large precomputed tables, reading them at locations determined by the data and key. Because the access location depended on the key, attacks inferring the key from cache hit and miss timing became known. Dedicated instructions compute in constant time inside the circuit without tables, so they are both faster and immune to this kind of side-channel leakage.
choiceNotes: The key length does not change.
Correct. Computation happens in constant time inside the circuit.
Cryptographic strength is unchanged.

hw-security-044.question: What must be observed when implementing cryptographic code in constant time?
choices: The whole operation must always finish in exactly one second
The clock must be stopped during processing
Branch directions, loop counts and memory addresses accessed must not depend on secret values
hw-security-044.explanation: Constant time means processing time does not vary with secret values. If a secret determines which way an if goes, timing changes; if a secret selects an array index, cache traces change. So code computes both outcomes and selects with bit operations instead of branching, and never indexes tables with secrets. It is also necessary to confirm that compiler optimizations do not reintroduce branches.
choiceNotes: It does not mean a fixed number of seconds.
The clock is not stopped.
Correct. It decouples timing and cache traces from secrets.

hw-security-045.question: What is the idea of partitioning a shared cache as a countermeasure to cache side channels?
choices: Physically splitting the cache in two and discarding it
Doubling the cache capacity
Assigning separate cache regions to processes or VMs so they cannot evict each other's data, making traces unobservable
hw-security-045.explanation: Cache side channels work because attacker and victim contend for the same cache locations. Assigning certain ways or sets of the cache to each process or VM prevents them from evicting each other's data, so the other party's access traces cannot be observed. Some CPUs offer features to control cache allocation. Each party gets less capacity, though, so it is a trade-off with performance.
choiceNotes: It is not physical splitting.
More capacity still leaves traces if shared.
Correct. In exchange, each gets less cache.

hw-security-046.question: Why do some systems handling confidential work disable the CPU's simultaneous multithreading (SMT)?
choices: Two threads on the same core share the L1 cache, execution units and more, so one thread can closely observe the other's activity
Disabling SMT always increases CPU performance
SMT cannot perform cryptographic computation
hw-security-046.explanation: With SMT, two threads run simultaneously in one core, finely sharing the L1 cache, branch predictor, execution units, buffers and more. One thread can therefore observe the resources the other uses through timing measurements, and several vulnerabilities required exactly this condition. To avoid sharing a core with untrusted parties, SMT is turned off or only threads of the same tenant are scheduled on the same core.
choiceNotes: Correct. The finer the sharing, the easier the leakage.
Total throughput usually drops.
Cryptographic computation works.

hw-security-047.question: What countermeasure protects against external devices connected to a PC using DMA to read or write main memory without permission?
choices: Raise the supply voltage of the external device
Make DMA transfers faster
Use an IOMMU to limit each device's DMA to memory regions the OS has permitted
hw-security-047.explanation: DMA lets devices read and write memory directly without the CPU, so a malicious or compromised device can read or modify OS memory and keys. This became a particular concern for devices attached through fast external ports. With an IOMMU, the OS restricts each device to the addresses it has allowed, and DMA to other locations is rejected.
choiceNotes: Voltage is irrelevant.
Faster transfers do not prevent it.
Correct. It applies address translation and protection per device.

hw-security-048.question: What is the idea of "defense in depth," emphasized in hardware and software security?
choices: Choosing only the single strongest countermeasure and omitting the rest
Layering several different countermeasures so the whole is not breached even if one fails
Doing nothing and thinking only after an attack
hw-security-048.explanation: Every countermeasure may have weaknesses not yet discovered. Defense in depth layers different kinds of protection, such as secure boot, memory protection, TEEs, encryption, side-channel countermeasures and physical tamper resistance, so that when one is breached the next layer still holds. The cost and effort for an attacker to defeat every layer at once is what makes the whole secure.
choiceNotes: If that one fails, everything fails.
Correct. It assumes no single measure is perfect.
Advance countermeasures are needed.

hw-security-049.question: When manufacturing many devices, why give each device its own key instead of the same key in all of them?
choices: So that even if one device is analyzed and its key extracted, the compromise does not spread to other devices
Different keys make devices run faster
Manufacturing equipment cannot handle identical keys
hw-security-049.explanation: If every device shares the same key, an attacker who obtains one unit and spends the time and money to extract the key endangers every device of that product. With per-device keys, a breach affects only that unit, and only its key needs revoking. Per-device keys are provisioned securely through PUFs, eFuse programming or key injection during manufacturing.
choiceNotes: Correct. It confines the damage to one device.
It has nothing to do with speed.
It is not a manufacturing equipment issue.

hw-security-050.question: When a CPU hardware vulnerability is discovered, which is one countermeasure applied to CPUs already shipped?
choices: Recalling all CPUs and replacing transistors one by one
Updating the CPU microcode to change problematic internal behavior or add new controls the OS can use
Changing the marking on the CPU surface
hw-security-050.explanation: Many CPUs implement complex instructions and some internal control in updatable microcode. When a vulnerability is found, the vendor distributes a microcode update loaded at every boot through the BIOS or OS. This can suppress problematic behavior or add new controls, such as instructions to flush branch predictors. Problems rooted in the circuitry itself are fixed fundamentally in the next CPU generation.
choiceNotes: Transistors cannot be replaced.
Correct. It is combined with OS and compiler countermeasures.
Changing the marking does not change behavior.
